query: We are investigating the atomic-scale thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy (HENA) nanoparticles synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane. The prevailing hypothesis is that high entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation. However, in situ heating experiments reveal a progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and a widening of the size distribution, alongside a reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries. Theoretical models based on Gibbs free energy often neglect surface energy terms critical for sub-10 nm systems. It has been observed that the FCC structure in these PLD-grown NPs may be governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy. Propose a mechanism explaining why atomic diffusion is surprisingly active in this quinary system, leading to the segregation of specific elements (like Au and Cu) to the surface and subsequent evaporation. Identify the critical temperature threshold where this mechanism becomes dominant, establish the boundary conditions regarding the initial nanoparticle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron), and formulate a falsification experiment involving simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic simulations to test if surface energy gradients alone can explain the observed phase separation without invoking sluggish diffusion.

generation.hypothesis: In AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, atomic diffusion is surprisingly active due to surface energy gradients driving element-specific segregation (Au and Cu preferentially to the surface), which overrides the sluggish diffusion effect predicted by bulk thermodynamics. This segregation is kinetically driven by the high surface-to-volume ratio in sub-5 nm particles, where surface energy minimization dominates over configurational entropy stabilization. The critical temperature threshold where this mechanism becomes dominant is approximately 600–800 K, below which the FCC structure is kinetically trapped but above which surface diffusion accelerates, leading to particle reshaping (elliptical to spherical), coalescence, and evaporation of low-surface-energy elements (Au, Cu). The initial nanoparticle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) influences the surface energy landscape: icosahedral particles with higher surface strain exhibit faster segregation and evaporation compared to truncated octahedra with lower surface energy facets. A falsification experiment would involve simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic simulations to test if surface energy gradients alone can explain phase separation without invoking sluggish diffusion, by comparing systems with identical bulk composition but varying surface terminations.
generation.material_initial_state: AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (sub-5 nm) synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane, initially exhibiting FCC structure with elliptical or icosahedral/truncated octahedral geometries.
generation.intervention: In situ heating experiments to observe thermal behavior, coupled with atomistic simulations to model surface energy-driven segregation and diffusion.
generation.conditions: Temperatures ranging from room temperature to 1000 K, vacuum or inert atmosphere, sub-5 nm particle size regime, silicon nitride substrate.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface energy gradients and element-specific surface segregation (Au, Cu enrichment at surface) leading to kinetic destabilization of the FCC structure.
generation.mechanism: Surface energy minimization drives preferential segregation of low-surface-energy elements (Au, Cu) to the nanoparticle surface, enhancing local diffusion rates and triggering evaporation. This kinetic process overrides the sluggish diffusion effect typically associated with high-entropy alloys, leading to particle reshaping, coalescence, and size distribution widening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles, widening of size distribution, reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries, and surface enrichment of Au and Cu, with critical onset at 600–800 K.
generation.baseline: Prevailing hypothesis that high entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation.
generation.boundary: Mechanism dominant in sub-10 nm nanoparticles; less relevant for bulk or larger particles where surface-to-volume ratio is low. Initial shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) modulates the rate of segregation and evaporation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact critical temperature threshold may vary with particle size, substrate interaction, and initial defect density. The relative contribution of surface energy vs. bulk thermodynamic effects requires further quantification.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations on AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles with controlled surface terminations (e.g., Au-rich vs. Cu-rich surfaces) at temperatures above and below the predicted threshold (600–800 K). If surface energy gradients alone explain phase separation, simulations should reproduce observed segregation and evaporation without invoking sluggish diffusion parameters. Deviations would indicate additional kinetic or thermodynamic factors.

First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.
